questions.q: Why does this lesson normalize Sentinel incidents and ASFF findings into a common record shape before correlating them?
options: Because boto3 requires all data to be in dictionary form
Because the two sources have different nested schemas (relatedEntities vs. Resources[].Details), and correlation logic needs one consistent shape to compare against, regardless of source
Because Sentinel incidents cannot be stored in Python variables otherwise
Because normalization is required by the Microsoft Graph API's terms of service
questions.explain: Sentinel and ASFF nest their data differently; normalizing both into the same flat shape (source, id, severity, ips, users) lets one correlation function work regardless of which cloud a record came from.

questions.q: How does the correlate() function in this lesson determine that a Sentinel incident and a Security Hub finding are related?
options: It calls a third-party threat-intelligence API to confirm the relationship
It checks whether their IDs are identical strings
It checks whether the set intersection of their IP addresses (s["ips"] & a["ips"]) is non-empty
It compares their severity labels for an exact match
questions.explain: correlate() computes a set intersection of each pair's IP sets; a non-empty shared_ips result means the two items share at least one concrete IP address.

questions.q: What does this lesson's correlation script deliberately NOT do, in keeping with the "automate the pipeline, gate the action" principle from Chapter 1?
options: It does not run at all unless a human manually triggers every single comparison
It does not use boto3 or the Sentinel APIs covered earlier in the chapter
It does not include severity information in its output
It does not take any containment action (closing the incident, isolating a host, blocking an IP) -- it only produces a decision-ready report of correlated pairs
questions.explain: The script stops at producing a list of correlated matches with both IDs, both severities, and the shared indicator -- leaving the decision about what the correlation means, and any resulting action, to a human analyst.

questions.q: If you wanted to extend this lesson's correlation approach to match on shared usernames instead of IPs, what would you change?
options: Intersect the "users" sets instead of (or in addition to) the "ips" sets -- the same set-intersection structure applies to any shared field
Nothing -- usernames are automatically correlated alongside IPs
You would need to rewrite correlate() using a completely different algorithm, such as machine learning
You would need to switch from Sentinel to a different SIEM entirely
questions.explain: The lesson notes that extending correlation to usernames or resource IDs is the same pattern -- intersecting a different field's set -- without changing the overall structure of correlate().

questions.q: In normalize_asff_finding(), where does the function look to find a finding's associated IP addresses?
options: In finding["Title"], by parsing the text for IP-shaped substrings
In finding["Resources"], drilling into each resource's Details.AwsEc2Instance.IpV4Addresses
It cannot find IP addresses from an ASFF finding at all
In a separate call to GuardDuty's list_findings()
questions.explain: normalize_asff_finding() loops through finding["Resources"] and collects IPv4 addresses nested under each resource's Details.AwsEc2Instance.IpV4Addresses field.
